Learning Objectives

  1. Define pain and describe the main types of nociceptors.
  2. Explain the anterolateral spinothalamic pain pathway (three-order-neuron chain).
  3. Differentiate fast and slow pain and their conducting fibers.
  4. Compare superficial, deep, and visceral pain.
  5. Explain referred pain and the convergence mechanism.
  6. Describe the pain gate control theory and the brain's descending analgesic system.
🧠

Definition of Pain

DefinitionPain is an unpleasant sensation produced by stimuli that cause, or threaten to cause, tissue damage (actual or potential tissue damage).

The essence of pain is tissue damage — any stimulus that causes or threatens to cause tissue damage triggers pain sensation. This is why pain receptors behave the way they do:

Why nociceptors barely adapt

Because the basis of pain is ongoing tissue damage, nociceptors are slow-adapting or non-adapting receptors. If the body "got used to" (adapted to) a damaging stimulus, the damage would be ignored and would keep worsening — so, by design, pain receptors keep signalling as long as the damaging stimulus persists.

Localization depends on receptor density

Localization accuracy depends on the number of receptors in a region. The skin and subcutaneous tissue are richly supplied with nociceptors, so cutaneous pain (e.g., a pin-prick) is sharply localized. The viscera have far fewer nociceptors, so visceral pain (e.g., abdominal pain) is typically diffuse and poorly localized.

FeatureSkin / Subcutaneous TissueViscera
Receptor densityHighLow
LocalizationAccurate, well-localizedDiffuse
⚡

Nociceptors & Types of Stimuli

Key conceptNociceptors are free nerve endings — every pain receptor is a free nerve ending. They detect potentially damaging mechanical, thermal, and chemical stimuli.

Chemical stimuli commonly arise from tissue injury: a cut releases prostaglandins, bradykinin, hydrogen ions (H⁺), and potassium (K⁺), all of which stimulate free nerve endings.

Four Types of Nociceptors (by stimulus)

Mechanical nociceptorsStimulated by mechanical energy — e.g. light tapping and traumatic pressure/injury.
Thermal nociceptorsActivated by temperature >42°C or by severe cold.
Chemical nociceptorsRespond to bradykinin, histamine, high acidity (H⁺), prostaglandin E2, potassium, etc.
Polymodal nociceptorsRespond to thermal, mechanical, and chemical stimuli together — unlike the other three, which are stimulus-specific.
Clinical Pearl — TRPV1Polymodal nociceptors are exemplified by TRPV1 (transient receptor potential vanilloid 1) channels. Eating hot peppers (capsaicin) activates TRPV1 and produces a burning, painful, "hot" sensation — even though no actual temperature rise has occurred. The channel is simply triggered chemically but reports as if it were a thermal stimulus.

The anterolateral spinothalamic tract, which carries pain, also carries temperature, crude touch, and crude pressure — relevant later for understanding analgesia and sensory overlap.

🔄

The Four Components of Pain

To feel pain, four sequential processes must occur:

① Transduction
Stimulus → action potential at the nociceptor
→
② Transmission
Action potential conducted along the pathway
→
③ Perception
Conscious recognition of pain (CNS)
→
④ Modulation
CNS dampens or amplifies the signal
ComponentWhat happens
TransductionMechanical, thermal, or chemical stimulus is converted into a receptor potential (local potential), which after summation triggers an action potential in the nociceptor (free nerve ending).
TransmissionThe action potential travels along the sensory pathway (nerve fibers) — i.e. along the anterolateral spinothalamic tract.
PerceptionThe signal reaches CNS centers where it is recognized/registered as pain.
ModulationThe CNS processes and regulates the pain signal — this is the basis of the descending analgesic system and gate control theory.
🧬

Anterolateral Spinothalamic Pathway (Transmission)

Pain transmission travels through a classic three-order-neuron chain:

1st-order neuron
Nociceptor → dorsal horn of spinal cord (via dorsal root ganglion)
→
2nd-order neuron
Synapses in dorsal horn → crosses to opposite side → ascends as the anterolateral spinothalamic tract → thalamus
→
3rd-order neuron
Thalamus → internal capsule → postcentral gyrus (somatosensory cortex)
Must-know — the crossing pointThe crossing (decussation) of the anterolateral spinothalamic tract occurs at the level of the spinal cord — NOT the brainstem. Specifically, it is the second-order neuron that crosses, immediately after synapsing with the first-order neuron in the dorsal horn.

Some second-order fibers give off collaterals to the brain stem reticular formation and to the non-specific (midline and intralaminar) thalamic nuclei. These non-specific projections to the sensory cortex produce general alertness/excitation rather than discriminative sensation.

Perception vs. LocalizationFull perception of pain occurs once the signal reaches the thalamus (some texts say awareness begins even at the spinal cord level). However, accurate localization of the pain requires the signal to reach the somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus).

The lateral spinothalamic tract (pain & temperature, right) vs. the dorsal column–medial lemniscal pathway (touch & proprioception, left) — both cross, but at different levels, and both converge on the thalamus → postcentral gyrus.

From the dorsal horn, pain input ascends to the thalamus (perception), with branches to the reticular formation (alertness) and hypothalamus/limbic system (emotional and behavioral responses to pain).

The First-Order Synapse & the Pain Gate

At the synapse between the first- and second-order neuron in the dorsal horn, the first-order neuron releases two key neurotransmitters:

Critical — memorize thisThe first-order neuron releases Glutamate and Substance P. These bind receptors on the second-order neuron, open ion channels, cause depolarization, and propagate the action potential onward — this is what allows perception and localization of pain to occur.

If glutamate and Substance P are not released, transmission of the pain signal does not occur. This is the physiological basis of the Pain Gate Theory.

Substantia gelatinosa — "the gate of pain"

The substantia gelatinosa is a layer of the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, referred to as the gate of pain. If something opens the gate, pain is transmitted and felt. If something closes the gate, analgesia results. The limbic system is also connected to this circuitry, explaining the emotional component that accompanies pain.

⚡

Fast vs. Slow Pain (Classification by Conduction Velocity)

By velocity of transmission, pain is classified into fast pain and slow pain — they differ in both the quality/nature of the sensation and the conduction velocity of their fibers.

FeatureFast PainSlow Pain
OnsetAcute — sudden onset, sudden offsetChronic, longer-lasting
SequenceFirst / immediateSecond — follows the fast/pricking pain
CharacterSharp, pricking, well-localizedDull, aching, burning, poorly localized (diffuse)
Fiber typeA delta (Aδ) fibers — large diameter, myelinatedC fibers — small diameter, unmyelinated
Conduction velocity12–30 m/s0.5–2 m/s
Classic exampleStick yourself with a pin/thorn: you first feel a sharp, well-localized pricking pain (fast, Aδ) — then moments later a duller, more diffuse ache spreads over the area (slow, C fibers).
🩺

Clinical Classification of Pain

Clinically, pain can also be divided into physiologic (acute) and pathologic (chronic) pain. Pathologic pain itself has two subtypes:

Nociceptive painResults from inflammation — the cause of pain has produced an inflammatory reaction outside the nervous system itself (tissue injury / inflammation stimulating intact nociceptors).
Neuropathic painThe problem lies in the nerve itself — direct damage, trauma, or lesion to the nerve (not simply stimulation of an intact nociceptor). Example: diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
TypePhysiologicPathologic → NociceptivePathologic → Neuropathic
DurationAcuteChronic
SourceNormal protective responseTissue inflammation (outside the nerve)Damage/lesion in the nerve itself
ExamplePin-prickInflammatory tissue injuryDiabetic peripheral neuropathy

Inflammatory pain: a lesion (e.g. a cut in the skin) releases bradykinin, serotonin, prostaglandins, histamine, and potassium — these stimulate free nerve endings (nociceptors) and produce pain.

🔍 Click to enlarge
Figure — Chemical Sensitization of Nociceptors

Tissue injury releases bradykinin and prostaglandins that sensitize/activate nociceptors, which release Substance P and CGRP; Substance P triggers mast-cell histamine release, and serotonin from platelets further activates nociceptors — the chemical basis of inflammatory (nociceptive) pain, hyperalgesia, and allodynia.

📍

Classification by Receptor Location: Superficial, Deep & Visceral

TypeReceptor locationFeatures
Superficial (cutaneous)Skin & subcutaneous tissueUsually well-localized (high receptor density). Often two components: an immediate sharp, highly-localized fast pain (Aδ), followed after ~1 second by a longer-lasting, more diffuse, delayed slow pain.
DeepMuscles, joints, ligaments, tendons, bonesLess rapid than cutaneous pain; usually poorly localized/diffuse.
VisceralViscera — lungs, liver, stomach, intestineLess rapid than cutaneous pain; poorly localized/diffuse; may be associated with nausea.

Deep & visceral pain — associated features

  • Autonomic reflexes: nausea, sweating, changes in heart rate and blood pressure.
  • Motor reflex — the "guarding" effect: muscles overlying a diseased viscus contract/stiffen to protect it from being touched or moved. Classic example: muscle guarding/stiffness over the RIF in appendicitis.
  • May be referred to a distant superficial site (see next section).

Causes of visceral pain

CauseMechanism
IschemiaReduced blood flow stimulates visceral nociceptors
Muscle spasmContraction of visceral smooth muscle
ObstructionMay lead to spasm and ischemia — e.g. renal and intestinal colic
Chemical stimuliGastric acid, pepsin, histamine, prostaglandins, bradykinin — e.g. gastric acid on a gastric ulcer
📡

Referred Pain

DefinitionReferred pain is visceral or deep pain felt at a superficial somatic site distant from the actual source of the stimulus.
Organ / SourceSite of Referred Pain
Heart (myocardial infarction)Inner aspect of the left arm
DiaphragmTip of the shoulder
Appendix (appendicitis)Peri-umbilical area (initially, before localizing to RIF)
Ureter (renal/ureteric colic)Testicle
🔀

Convergence Theory — Mechanism of Referred Pain

The accepted mechanism is the dermatomal rule / convergence theory:

  • In fetal life, a given viscus and a corresponding dermatome/segment share the same embryological origin/nature.
  • As the fetus grows, the viscus and the dermatome-related structure separate anatomically, but their nerve fibers retain the same central connections (the same "root").
  • Example: the heart and the inner aspect of the left arm were embryologically related; despite separating structurally, their afferents still converge on the same spinal segment.
The convergence stepVisceral (or deep) nociceptor afferents and cutaneous nociceptor afferents enter the same dorsal horn and converge onto the same second-order neuron.
Why the brain "gets it wrong" — error in projectionThe cortex is far more accustomed to receiving input from the skin than from the viscera (many more cutaneous afferents use this shared pathway). So when the shared second-order neuron is activated by visceral disease, the brain defaults to projecting the sensation to the skin/dermatome rather than to the true diseased viscus — an "error in projection."

Teaching analogy from the lecture: like blaming the "usual troublemaker" sibling whenever something breaks at home — the cortex is "used to" hearing from the skin, so it blames the skin.

🚪

Gate Control Theory of Pain

Core ideaPain crosses into the CNS through the "gate" at the substantia gelatinosa. This gate can be closed by a non-painful stimulus, blocking the transmission of pain.

Classic example: rubbing an injury

When someone hits their hand, they instinctively rub the area. Rubbing is a non-painful stimulus that activates A beta (Aβ) fibers — large, fast tactile fibers, faster than both Aδ and C fibers.

Touch / rubbing
Activates A beta fibers (fastest)
→
Touch signal arrives first
Reaches dorsal horn ahead of the pain signal
→
Activates inhibitory interneurons
Release enkephalins
→
Gate closes
Delayed pain signal is blocked; brain perceives touch, not pain

Because the touch signal (Aβ) is faster than the pain signal (Aδ/C), it reaches the dorsal horn first, triggers inhibitory interneurons that release enkephalins, and closes the gate before the pain signal arrives — the brain receives the touch signal instead of the pain signal.

💊

Descending Analgesic (Modulation) System

Beyond gate control by peripheral touch input, the brain has its own descending pain-inhibitory system. This underlies phenomena like stress-induced analgesia — e.g. an athlete injured mid-game may not feel pain until the game/stress is over.

Key structures

  • Periaqueductal gray matter (PAG) and the raphe magnus nucleus send descending fibers to the dorsal horn that produce inhibition.
  • Descending fibers release serotonin or catecholamines (as occurs with stress activation).
  • These excite inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn, which release opioids — specifically enkephalins and endorphins.
  • Enkephalins/endorphins bind opioid receptors present on the first-order neuron and inhibit release of Substance P and glutamate — closing the pain gate. Because transmission is blocked (modulation acting on transmission), perception never occurs.
🔍 Click to enlarge
Figure — Descending Pathways

The periaqueductal gray (midbrain) projects to the nucleus raphe magnus/rostral ventromedial medulla, which sends serotonergic and catecholaminergic fibers down to the dorsal horn to inhibit incoming afferent pain fibers.

🔍 Click to enlarge
Figure — Opioid Blockade of Transmission

(a) A noxious stimulus normally drives Substance-P release onto dorsal horn excitatory interneurons. (b) Endogenous opiates released by descending analgesic pathways bind opiate receptors on the afferent terminal, block Substance P release, and stop transmission of the pain signal to the thalamus — "no perception of pain."

Clinical application — pharmacology

Opioids (e.g. morphine)Mimic enkephalins/endorphins at presynaptic opiate receptors on the first-order neuron, blocking Substance P/glutamate release. Very potent, but use is limited by addiction risk.
NSAIDsAct peripherally — inhibit the formation of prostaglandins from damaged tissue, reducing nociceptor stimulation (rather than acting on opiate receptors centrally).
⭐

High-Yield Exam Pearls

  • Nociceptors are free nerve endings, non-adapting/slow-adapting — so the body keeps reacting to ongoing tissue damage.
  • Transduction = converting a mechanical/thermal/chemical stimulus into an action potential. Transmission = conducting that action potential along the spinothalamic tract.
  • The first-order neuron releases glutamate and Substance P at the dorsal horn (substantia gelatinosa) to propagate the signal to the second-order neuron.
  • The second-order neuron crosses at the level of the spinal cord, not the brainstem.
  • A delta fibers: large, myelinated, fast/acute pain (pricking, sharp, well-localized), 12–30 m/s.
  • C fibers: small, unmyelinated, slow/chronic pain (dull, aching, burning, poorly localized), 0.5–2 m/s.
  • Full perception occurs at the thalamus; accurate localization requires the signal to reach the somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus).
  • Referred pain = convergence theory — visceral and cutaneous fibers share the same dorsal horn/second-order neuron; the brain (used to skin input) falsely projects the pain to the skin.
  • Gate control theory: rubbing activates fast, large A beta tactile fibers, which reach the dorsal horn before pain fibers and activate inhibitory interneurons (releasing enkephalins) that close the gate (substantia gelatinosa) to incoming pain signals.
🩺

Clinical Pearls

TRPV1 activationPatients eating hot peppers (capsaicin) feel burning pain not from an actual temperature rise, but because capsaicin directly activates TRPV1 channels (polymodal nociceptors).
Referred pain patternsMI → inner left arm · Diaphragmatic irritation → tip of shoulder · Appendicitis → peri-umbilical area initially → later localizes to RIF · Renal/ureteric colic → testicle.
Visceral/deep pain autonomic responsesOften accompanied by nausea, sweating, and changes in blood pressure/heart rate.
Guarding effectIn appendicitis, somatic muscles overlying the inflamed viscus reflexively contract (stiffness) to protect it.
Pain managementOpioids bind presynaptic opioid receptors on the first-order neuron in the dorsal horn, blocking Substance P/glutamate release — effectively closing the pain gate.
Neuropathic vs. nociceptive painNeuropathic pain (e.g. diabetic peripheral neuropathy) arises from direct damage/lesion to the nerve itself — distinguish it from nociceptive pain, which arises from external tissue inflammation stimulating an intact nerve.

Key concepts من الموضوع ده، إنه الـ nociceptors detect potentially damaging mechanical, thermal, and chemical stimuli. الـ damage ده ممكن يكون من stimuli mechanical صحيح؟ صح؟ زول ضربتك حاجة، يعني إنت ماشي يا اخوانا مثلا خبطت في التيبل في الطرابيزة دي، دي mechanical. ممكن thermal، thermal طبعا فيها اتنين، فيها cold وفيها hot stimuli. يعني لو مسكت ثلج لفترة شوية طويلة بتحس بـ pain صح؟ لو هبشت حاجة حارة بتحس بـ pain. فدي الـ thermal stimuli، فالـ pain receptors بتستجيب لـ different types of stimuli اللي هي ممكن تكون mechanical، ممكن تكون thermal، وممكن تكون chemical stimuli.

Polymodal.

الـ mechanical nociceptors stimulated by mechanical energy زي الـ light tapping and traffic trauma. Okay؟ الـ thermal nociceptors activated by temperature above 42 degree centigrade or severe cold. الـ polymodal، هي عبارة عن nociceptors بتستجيب لمجموعة من الـ stimuli مع بعض، يعني مثلا يا اخوانا الـ chemical nociceptors ما بتستجيب للـ temperature stimulation واضح؟ الـ chemical nociceptors ما بتستجيب للـ mechanical stimulation، لكن الـ polymodal عندها القدرة تستجيب للـ thermal، mechanical، or chemical stimuli. عشان كده سموها polymodal متعددة الـ modes اوكي؟ polymodal.

واضح؟ فبتحس بـ pain وبتحس بـ thermal stimulation. فالزول لما تلقاه بياكل شطة بيعمل كده صح؟ actual هو ما في حرارة، اوكي؟ واضحة يا اخوانا؟ ده مثال للـ polymodal nociceptors. معايا يا شباب؟ متأكدين؟ طيب.

Endorphins and enkephalins. الـ endorphins والـ enkephalins بيشتغلوا على الـ first order neuron، بيعملوا ليه inhibition، وبالتالي بيعملوا inhibition للـ release of glutamate and substance P. معناها البوابة ما حتتفتح.

الـ descending fibers تفرز سيروتونين أو كاتيكولامينز زي ما في الـ stress. These excite inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn. Interneurons release opioids such as enkephalins and endorphins. These bind to opioid receptors that present in the first order neuron of the pain pathway. الـ opioids دي لما ترتبط بالريسبترات بتاعتها، بتمنع الـ release بتاع substance P والـ glutamate. وبالتالي الـ pain sensation بيقيف هنا.

يعني في الـ pain، إحنا قلنا عشان الـ pain كله الـ components بتاعته transduction, transmission, perception, modulation. الـ modulation ده وقف لي الـ perception of pain في الـ transmission. الـ transmission ما اكتملت. فعشان كده ما في perception.

يا اخوانا الـ pain killers دي كلها مسكنات الألم ممكن تشتغل بالطريقة دي في الـ opiate receptors. المورفين بيشتغل هنا. لكن لأن المورفين بنخاف منه للـ addiction، فعشان كده استخدامه limited. لكن هو very potent pain killer. الـ pain killers دي بتشتغل بنفس الطريقة دي في الـ opiate receptors، وممكن الـ NSAIDs تشتغل في المواد اللي بتتفرز من الـ tissue damage وتمنع تكوينها زي الـ prostaglandins وتمنع الـ stimulation of nociceptors.

الـ opioid receptors اللي هي موجودة وين؟ موجودة في الـ first order neuron بتاع الـ pain pathway. أول ما الأوبيويدز دي اللي هي الـ enkephalin والـ endorphin ترتبط بالريسبترات بتاعتها، بتعمل inhibition للـ release of substance P and glutamate. وبالتالي البوابة مقتولة، معناها مافي pain sensation.

النظرية دي اللي هي دي اسمها الـ Gate Control Theory. Gate control theory يا اخوانا فكرتها شنو؟ الـ pain بيعبر بالبوابة دي. إنت تقدر تقفل البوابة دي بـ non-painful stimulus. مثلا زول اتضرب في يده، طوالي بيعمل شنو؟ بيمسح عليها صح؟ الـ rubbing ده non-painful stimulus، بيشتغل على A beta fibers. الـ A beta fibers large tactile fibers، أسرع من الـ A delta وأسرع من الـ C fibers.

فلما تعمل rubbing، الإشارة بتاعت الـ touch بتصل الـ dorsal horn أسرع، وبتحفز inhibitory interneurons عشان تطلع enkephalins وتقفل البوابة قدام إشارة الألم الجاية متأخرة. فالـ brain بيستقبل الإشارة بتاعت الـ touch وما بيستقبل الإشارة بتاعت الـ pain. ده الأساس بتاع الـ Gate Control Theory of Pain.

في مشكلة؟ خلصنا المحاضرة.
